description: We are a team of Computer Science and Computer Engineering students who developed Lunite, a web-based platform that simplifies the selection and comparison of potential lunar landing sites through interactive visualizations and mission-specific data.
summary:
Lunite is a web platform that lets mission planners, educators, and the public compare lunar landing sites and dates in seconds. Why did we build it? Because the information needed to evaluate a landing site is scattered across different tools and the existing tools for planning a lunar landing have a structure that makes them slow to use and hard to share beyond specialist teams. The result? the process becomes inefficient, and the decision-making process slows down.

Lunite closes that gap. It brings that information together in one place. With a simple, intuitive interface, users go from accessible mission planning, through unique 3D visualizations of relevant data to be compared, to comparisons and results that can be shared easily.

Our vision is a platform where planners, educators, and the public analyze and compare landing sites using the same data and the same visual language. We stay close to our users, which is why simplicity, organization, and creativity drive our design: not just faster site evaluation, but wider access to lunar knowledge for everyone.
details:
THE PROBLEM

The tools available today for evaluating lunar landing sites, such as Quickmap, Moon Trek, and JPL Horizons, were built for detailed analysis, but their results are locked behind complex interfaces that make them hard to use whether for specialists or for the general public.

The main obstacle is that the information is scattered: to evaluate each combination of site and date, a planner has to navigate several interfaces, extract raw data from each one, and cross-reference it manually. Ephemeris and topographic data arrive untranslated, rather than as clear, comparable visualizations, which slows down scenario comparison exactly when it is needed most. Schedules shift and hardware gets delayed, and teams must reassess sites and dates quickly, yet there is no accessible tool to support that kind of agile planning.

The result is a gap between the abundance of technical data and the real ability to use it for decision-making, one that also keeps educators and the general public from understanding how a lunar landing is planned. That gap weighs even more heavily at the Moon's south pole, where many future missions are planned because of the presence of water ice. There, the terrain's geometry produces extreme variations in lighting and Earth visibility across lunar days and seasons, so small changes in site or date dramatically alter the available power and the communication windows.

WHAT OUR SOLUTION DOES

Lunite is a web tool that turns raw lunar data into an answer to one question: where, and when, can we land? The planner describes the mission once, choosing a curated site or any point on a 3D globe of the Moon, then setting probe parameters, dates, mission duration, allowed launch delay and tolerances for sunlight and communication. For each candidate point around the site, Lunite uses NASA's LOLA terrain and JPL Horizons positions of the Sun and Earth to compute the share of time in sunlight, the share with direct Earth communication, the longest darkness and the longest blackout. Valid points appear as vertical bars over the real 3D terrain, filtered and compared side by side, and the best candidates can be exported in a PDF report to share with the team.

This solves the problem by putting terrain and ephemeris in one place and translating them into percentages, hours and bars that specialists and non-specialists can read. When the schedule slips, Lunite slides the mission window day by day, fixes the best one and says which requirement to relax if nothing works. It also respects the south pole's sensitivity, with terrain resolution down to 10–40 m, real horizons that include the Moon's curvature, and landing precision as a parameter.

OUR DIFFERENTIALS

Lunite lets users compare periods and see how viable each site is in each one, while choosing only the metrics they care about. The data is shown in an intuitive way, through vertical bars that represent each site’s information.

What does that mean in practice?

Periods, not just places.

Launch dates change, and a site that works today may not work two weeks later. Lunite is built to answer “what if we land later?” as easily as “what if we land somewhere else?”. Users can see how the same site performs across different dates, and not only how one site compares with another. 

The user is in control, the visualization is unique and the data explains itself.

When the viable landing sites for a region are loaded, the user chooses one or more metrics that matter for the mission, such as sunlight duration or Earth visibility windows. Lunite displays vertical bars, one for each site, that show at a glance how well each one satisfies the selected metric (or set of metrics). Instead of opening several tools and cross-referencing numbers by hand, the planner quickly sees which sites stand out, and even non-specialists can interpret the chart.

From this overview, filters narrow the list of candidates further, discarding sites that fail requirements such as a minimum of power generation or Earth communication, which speeds up decision-making and avoids wasting time on unviable options. Finally, the user compares two sites side by side, fixing one and choosing another, or sequentially, stepping through the sites as a list. In both cases, the data is handpicked, only what truly matters for the decision, which makes the process much easier and more efficient.

Everything in one place: a simple and intuitive interface. 

Lunite brings together the data of all landing sites on a single platform, with a simple and intuitive interface. Users do not need to cross-reference information manually across different tools, which makes assessing viability and selecting the most suitable site less complex and more efficient. 

Shareable

Upon completing the analysis, users can generate a report detailing the specifics of the selected landing sites. This document allows a quick comparison of the strongest candidates and can be shared with the rest of the team, supporting the final decision on the landing site.

OUR IMPACT

Our mission starts from a simple observation: the solutions available today for choosing a landing site are too complex and too scattered. Lunite’s impact comes from reversing that, in three ways.

  • For mission planners, Lunite shortens the path between a changed constraint and a new decision. When a launch slips or hardware changes, teams can quickly identify a viable alternative site or date, and science and engineering teams can discuss the same visual evidence instead of translating between different tools.
  • For educators and students, Lunite turns ephemeris and topographic data into something that can be seen and explored. Rather than explaining in the abstract why the Moon’s south pole is so demanding, a teacher can show the Sun and Earth over the horizon and let students change the date themselves.
  • For the general public, Lunite lowers the barrier to understanding lunar exploration. Anyone can ask where and when a landing could work and receive an answer they can read, without specialist training.

As a result, Lunite leaves a clear legacy: solving the decentralization of lunar knowledge. By bringing it together in one place, with the same data and the same visual language for everyone, it allows more people to access it. Simplicity, organization, and creativity guide how we get there, and staying close to our users keeps us moving in the right direction.
